title: DoorDash Uses Multi Agent LLMs to Clean up 60,000 Feature Flags
gist: DoorDash built a two-phase multi-agent system using Claude Sonnet and Opus via Google's Agent Development Kit to clean up stale feature flags, producing usable pull requests for 45 of 50 evaluated flags at an average of 13.8 minutes and $4.79 each versus one to two hours of manual work, with zero reported regressions.

insights.claim: DoorDash's experimentation platform manages more than 60,000 feature flags across roughly 623 repositories and creates about 2,300 new flags each month, with more than 1,000 flags identified as stale.
insights.speaker: Leela Kumili
insights.so_what: At this creation rate, manual flag cleanup was structurally unsustainable, which is the business case for automating it rather than just a technical curiosity.
insights.locator: DoorDash's experimentation platform manages more than 60,000 feature flags

insights.claim: DoorDash defines a feature flag as stale when it has not been modified for 90 days, remains referenced in code, is not archived or retired, and is not explicitly excluded, and a daily process automatically creates Jira tickets for flags meeting this definition.
insights.speaker: Leela Kumili
insights.so_what: A precise, automatable staleness definition is the prerequisite that makes downstream agentic cleanup tractable at all.
insights.locator: A flag is classified as stale when it has not been modified

insights.claim: DoorDash's use of dependency-injected wrappers means a flag's definition, client call, and business logic can be distributed across multiple files, so cleaning up a single Boolean flag can require changes across five to 20 files, including tests.
insights.speaker: Leela Kumili
insights.so_what: This scattering of logic is exactly why simple find-and-delete tooling fails and why the cleanup problem required something closer to code comprehension than pattern matching.
insights.locator: The cleanup is complicated by DoorDash's use of dependency-injected wrappers

insights.claim: Uber's open-source Piranha tool uses abstract syntax tree-based transformations to remove stale feature flag code, but DoorDash found this rule-based approach did not cover its dependency-injection pattern because the relationship between a flag and its application logic is semantic rather than directly represented by matching syntax.
insights.speaker: Leela Kumili
insights.so_what: Semantic, cross-file coupling is a case where rule-based AST tooling hits a ceiling and LLM-based reasoning becomes the more viable path, a pattern likely to recur in other large codebases with similar DI conventions.
insights.locator: Uber's open-source Piranha uses abstract syntax tree-based transformations

insights.claim: DoorDash's workflow, built on Google's Agent Development Kit, runs in two phases: an orchestrator running Claude Sonnet retrieves stale-flag tickets from Jira, searches relevant repositories, and queries the experimentation platform via Model Context Protocol for metadata including rollout percentage and target value, after which an engineer reviews the report and confirms the target value before any code changes begin.
insights.speaker: Leela Kumili
insights.so_what: Keeping a human confirmation gate before code generation, rather than after, limits the blast radius of a wrong target-value determination before any changes are made.
insights.locator: The DoorDash workflow uses Google's Agent Development Kit

insights.claim: In the second phase, DoorDash runs Claude Opus cleanup agents in isolated Git worktrees, with up to four agents running concurrently per repository, each with a one-hour timeout, and Gradle running without its daemon specifically to prevent state sharing between worktrees.
insights.speaker: Leela Kumili
insights.so_what: Isolating agent workspaces and disabling shared build-daemon state is a concrete pattern for safely running multiple concurrent coding agents against the same repository without cross-contamination.
insights.locator: During the second phase, Claude Opus cleanup agents operate

insights.claim: DoorDash's cleanup agents open a pull request only after the code passes builds, tests, JaCoCo patch coverage, and Detekt static analysis, meaning validation happens before a PR is even created rather than only at review or merge time.
insights.speaker: Leela Kumili
insights.so_what: Gating PR creation on automated validation reduces reviewer burden by ensuring every PR an engineer sees has already cleared a baseline quality bar.
insights.locator: A pull request is opened only after the validation checks pass

insights.claim: In an evaluation of 50 stale flags, DoorDash's multi-agent system produced usable pull requests for 45 of them, averaging 13.8 minutes and $4.79 per cleanup, compared with DoorDash's own estimate of one to two hours for manual cleanup.
insights.speaker: Leela Kumili
insights.so_what: A concrete per-task cost ($4.79) and time (13.8 minutes) for agentic code cleanup gives a real benchmark for ROI modeling of similar agentic engineering automation elsewhere.
insights.locator: In an evaluation of 50 stale flags, the system produced usable pull requests

insights.claim: Success rates in DoorDash's evaluation degraded predictably with logic complexity: simple flags achieved a 100% single-pass cleanup rate, medium-complexity flags 94%, and complex flags 85%, with the five cases requiring engineer intervention driven by deep call chains and cross-interface parameter threading.
insights.speaker: Leela Kumili
insights.so_what: A clear complexity-to-success-rate gradient lets teams predict which flag classes are safe to fully automate versus which still need human review, informing where to expand automation first.
insights.locator: Simple flags achieved a 100% single-pass cleanup rate

insights.claim: The 50-flag evaluation produced 31 first-pass merges, 14 revisions, and five engineer interventions, and DoorDash reported no bugs or regressions across all 50 evaluated changes.
insights.speaker: Leela Kumili
insights.so_what: A zero-regression outcome across 50 live production changes is the key evidence needed to justify expanding an agentic cleanup system beyond a pilot.

insights.claim: DoorDash plans to add confidence scoring for lower-risk cleanups and a post-cleanup code quality pass to catch issues such as misleading variable names left behind after a flag is removed.
insights.speaker: Leela Kumili
insights.so_what: Adding a code-quality pass on top of passing tests acknowledges that build/test success alone doesn't guarantee clean code, a maturity signal for how far to trust current agentic guardrails.
insights.locator: The company plans to add confidence scoring

insights.claim: DoorDash's feature flag cleanup work was accepted for the ICSME 2026 industry track.
insights.speaker: Leela Kumili
insights.so_what: Academic-conference acceptance lends independent, peer-reviewed credibility to the reported results rather than resting solely on a company blog post.
insights.locator: The work was accepted for the ICSME 2026 industry track
